title: SSE output sharding reconciliation and offline function-call handoff
creator: Priya Shah
description: Problem: Long-running SSE streams that produce structured outputs and function/tool call signals are being split into multiple small network frames. During client reconnects or partial retries we currently struggle to guarantee: 1) deterministic reassembly of structured output (JSON objects, function_call blocks) without duplicating side-effects; 2) safe handoff of pending function calls when the original streaming session is interrupted; and 3) graceful behavior for legacy clients that do not implement the newer resume protocol. This ticket proposes an end-to-end design for sharding output into reconcileable fragments, an idempotent/offline function-call handoff flow, and a compatibility layer for older clients.
acceptance_criteria: Server emits shard metadata for each fragment: stream_id, shard_seq, shard_count (when known), payload_checksum
Upon reconnect with resume token, server replays only missing shards and guarantees structured output assembly equals original logical event stream

Function calls that were emitted but not confirmed are either executed exactly-once or gated by idempotency tokens; offline handoff moves pending function calls to a durable queue and notifies caller of new execution handle
Legacy clients (no resume token support) receive a backward-compatible summary event containing reassembled structured outputs and clear function_call markers
End-to-end integration tests pass: reconnect+resume, late-ACK, duplicate-frames, and function-call replay scenarios
Telemetry exists: shard loss rate, reorder rate, function-call handoff rate, duplicate function executions
design_notes: High-level approach: 1) Shard format: each SSE data block will include a small JSON prefix (base64 optional) with {stream_id, shard_id, seq, checksum, flags}. Payload can be binary or text. 2) Reconciliation: server maintains a short-lived per-stream fragment index (in-memory with optional redis backing) to map seq -> payload and compute deterministic reassembly. On reconnect the client provides resume_token (last_seq_ack). Server replies with missing shards and a final 'shard_end' event when the logical message completes. 3) Function-call handoff: when an outgoing structured event contains a function_call directive, runtime attaches a function_call_token and writes a durable handoff entry (function_call_token -> serialized call + idempotency_key) to the function queue. If session persists, the function executes immediately. If session is interrupted, the handoff entry is claimed by the offline runner using the token; the runner posts status updates to the stream and emits a 'function_result' shard when done. 4) Idempotency: function callers must supply idempotency_key optional; if absent, runtime generates a deterministic key derived from stream_id + logical_event_seq. 5) Backwards compatibility: for clients that do not understand shard metadata, the server will emit an extra legacy 'atomic' event when a logical message finishes, containing the assembled JSON and a simplified function_call placeholder (function_call_url) rather than token-based handoff. 6) Resource controls: shard window limits per stream, TTL for fragment index (default 2 minutes), max shards per logical message (default 256).
rollout_plan: Internal dogfood: enable for internal services and a small set of customers using dedicated infra
Canary: enable for 5% of hosted API traffic with telemetry gating
Observe metrics for 72 hours; rollback if duplicate function executions exceed threshold or reorder rates spike
Gradual ramp after fixes and safety hardening
test_plan: Unit tests for shard serializer/deserializer and checksum mismatch handling
Integration test harness simulating TCP drops, delayed reconnects, and out-of-order shard delivery
Chaos test: kill server mid-logical-event and validate function-call handoff to offline runner
Compatibility tests: legacy client that only consumes 'atomic' events must see identical logical output
Load test: verify memory/redis index scales with thousands of concurrent streams and shard retention TTL
implementation_tasks: runtime: emit shard metadata header and event types (shard, shard_end, function_handoff, function_result)
runtime: fragment index service with optional redis persistence and eviction policy
runtime: durable function handoff queue and offline runner claim protocol
api: resume token semantics documented in API spec and SDKs; SDK helpers for generating idempotency keys
console: add per-stream debug view showing shard timeline and handoff status
sdk: JS/Go client: support resume token exchange and automatic reassembly; provide 'legacyMode' boolean
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Duplicate function execution due to race between live executor and offline runner. Mitigation: require claiming step with compare-and-swap using function_call_token and idempotency_key. Log and emit event if duplicate execution detected.
Risk: Increased memory pressure from fragment index. Mitigation: strict TTL and configurable shard_count limits; fallback to 'atomic' summarization when limits exceeded.
Risk: Legacy clients misinterpreting metadata leading to broken parsing. Mitigation: send legacy 'atomic' event in parallel until adoption reaches threshold.
Risk: Performance impact on p99 latency for tiny responses. Mitigation: bypass sharding for payloads < 4KB and for low-latency routes; provide sampling to monitor overhead.
open_questions: Q1: What default idempotency key derivation is safest across multi-region routing? (request_hash vs stream_seq)
Q2: Should function handoff tokens be short-lived JWTs or opaque UUIDs stored server-side?
Q3: Can we reuse existing resume_token semantics or introduce a separate shard_resume token to simplify compatibility?
Q4: Operational cost: should fragment index use redis cluster or a memory-backed LRU with redis as overflow?
